title: Backend Trust in Unverified Upstream Validation or Authorization
pattern: A backend endpoint or service assumes frontend, gateway, or upstream-proxy checks make incoming arguments safe and omits its own required input validation or authorization decision.
why_bad: Direct requests bypass client-side checks, and a compromised upstream service can invoke backend RPCs with spoofed user parameters, causing unauthorized reads or mutations of any user's records [30:235]. Structurally valid data can still be unauthorized, and authorized callers can still supply malformed data.
detection: Endpoint case: administrative or state-mutating handlers act on untrusted resource identifiers or values without enforcing structural constraints, authentication where required, and the authenticated caller's permission for that specific resource and action [30:235]. RPC case: a backend service method trusts a supplied user identifier or frontend assertion without validating a trusted end-user context in the call and independently checking the requested access; this includes reads as well as writes.
fix: Enforce structural validation and authentication/authorization appropriate to every backend endpoint regardless of upstream client checks [30:235]. Across the RPC trust boundary, propagate a cryptographically signed End-User Context (EUC) ticket or equivalent authenticated context from the frontend, verify it at the backend, and use the verified identity to enforce the resource/action policy. Do not accept identity verification as a substitute for authorization.
source: *Building Secure and Reliable Systems* (Adkins), Chapter 5; *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* (Vernon), Chapter 14 [30:235]; `Heather Adkins et al. - Building Secure and Reliable Systems (2020)`, Ch 6, p. 109-110.
